title: Teach Microduck to score a goal
text: What you will build  Use one Microduck, one ball and one goal to connect motion, simulation and learning with engineered pipelines, learned policies and task agents. Chapters 1–5 retain existing labs, Chapter 6 reviews the baseline, and Chapters 7–9 explain frontier methods and readiness. New-method football training has not yet been completed here.    1 Motion and learning foundations   2 Review the engineered baseline   3 Learn actions with GR00T   4 Organize tasks with ASPIRE   5 Expand environments with Cosmos and Isaac     By the end, you can   Explain mechanisms, actuators, observations, actions and rewards.  Explore fixed policies and learning with Isaac Lab, Newton and Isaac Sim.  Distinguish engineered pipelines, VLA actions and task agents.  Adapt the SO-101 data workflow to Microduck demonstration/action requirements.  Design variation and held-out evaluation; distinguish readiness from task success.     Course route      Chapter  Task      Chapter 1  Meet Microduck: play football first    Chapter 2  Mechanism and control timing    Chapter 3  Learning to walk    Chapter 4  Adapt walking to slopes    Chapter 5  Explore community movement skills    Chapter 6  From engineered pipelines to intelligent robots    Chapter 7  Teach GR00T from demonstrations    Chapter 8  Organize tasks and accumulate skills with ASPIRE    Chapter 9  Cover different homes with Cosmos and Isaac

title: How to take this course
text: Choose a learning path      Path  What you do  What you need      Observe  Read, inspect the 3D assembly, watch demonstrations, and answer checks.  A modern browser    Use fixed models (recommended)  Copy terminal commands, run simulation, and record observations.  A prepared GPU environment    Practice training  Add your own training, export, and evaluation.  Additional runtime and disk space      Start with the demonstrations, then optionally practice training in Chapters 3 and 4. Chapter 6 is an overview; Chapters 7–9 explain frontier methods and integration requirements without new framework installation or large-model training. All reading and browser interactions work without a GPU.    Prerequisites   Open a Linux terminal, change directories, and copy multiline commands.  Read basic Python functions, arrays, and parameters. Prior PPO knowledge is not required.  Understand positions, angles, and velocities; robot coordinate frames are introduced in the course.    About your training results  Your checkpoint is a practice artifact. Later chapters explicitly use the course models in  models/ ; they never select the latest training run automatically. Using your own policy requires an explicit checkpoint and a new evaluation.     A useful lab routine   Read the expected result before running a command.  Run commands from the repository root. Use a new output directory for every run.  Keep the command, seed, and result—including failures.  Answer the chapter check before moving on.   Reading and exercise durations are planning estimates, not training-time guarantees. The first launch may download assets, compile kernels, and populate rendering caches.

title: Prepare your environment
text:
Runtime requirements  The reference environment is Ubuntu 24.04 on DGX Spark (aarch64), Python 3.12, Isaac Sim 6, and pinned Isaac Lab / Newton revisions. Simulation uses Newton’s native actuator path. Other GPUs or versions may run, but the course results do not automatically apply to them.  You need an NVIDIA driver, a GPU-enabled graphical desktop, Git, Docker, and network access to NVIDIA package sources. None of these are required for reading the website. Review the Isaac Sim license before installing the simulator.    Download the course and models  Open a terminal in the directory where you want to keep the course, then run the commands below to clone and enter the repository.    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    mkdir -p "$HOME/microduck"
cd "$HOME/microduck"
git clone https://github.com/NV-DLI/Microduck-Workshop.git
cd Microduck-Workshop
python3 scripts/workshop.py verify-models    The models are included in the repository, so no Hugging Face login is required. The verification command checks every model’s SHA-256. Continue only when all files match. Course weights and student outputs are stored separately.    Workspace    Microduck-Workshop/
├── web/          # HTML course
├── lab/          # simulation and learning code
├── models/       # fixed course models
├── scripts/      # lab entry points
└── outputs/      # your runs (created when needed)      Prepare the simulator  First prepare system tools. The commands below install Git, Python virtual-environment support, and video encoding. Set up Docker using its  Ubuntu instructions ;  docker info  should show server information without a permission error.    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y git python3-venv ffmpeg
docker info
export UV_HTTP_TIMEOUT=600      Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py setup
python3 scripts/workshop.py doctor     setup  prepares the pinned runtime. If you already have a matching Isaac Lab checkout, bind it using  --isaaclab /path/to/IsaacLab .  doctor  checks Python, models, GPU, the desktop display setting, and navigation dependencies. Resolve failed checks before continuing.   Launch from your desktop terminal  Run GUI commands in a terminal on the GPU machine’s desktop. The website provides lessons and commands; Isaac opens in its own window. On the first launch, allow shaders and assets to finish loading.     Before you continue  Run the command below in a terminal at the repository root. If it specifies an output directory, use a new one to retain earlier results.    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py inspect-model --model models/walk.onnx    Expected result: input and output names, tensor shapes, and model identity. If the GPU is unavailable, use the troubleshooting page before proceeding. Keep the pinned physics backend and model combination.

title: Meet Microduck: play football first
text:
A small robot that learns new skills  Microduck is an open biped from Pollen Robotics and Hugging Face with 14 actuated joints. Start with the official walking and right-foot kick ONNX policies in Isaac Sim, then learn how Isaac Lab trains and evaluates new skills.    Open the pitch and try the keyboard      Walk toward the ball, stop, then switch to the right-foot kick.   Complete  setup  and run the command below from the repository root. Click the Isaac Sim window to focus it. The robot, ball and goal use the same dimensions and physical settings as the autonomous task. Use an English keyboard input mode so an IME does not consume movement keys.    Terminal  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py manual \
  --seconds 600 \
  --output outputs/manual-football-01        Key  Action      W / S  Forward / backward    A / D  Step left / right    Q / E  Turn left / right    Release movement keys  Stand with zero velocity command    Space  Right-foot kick, then stand    R / Esc  Restart / exit      Walk toward the ball, stop with the ball in front of the right foot, and face the goal before pressing Space. Reposition after a miss; press R after a fall. You choose the target and direction; the policies coordinate the joints.  Default standing is the walking policy responding to zero movement commands. Getting up after a fall, sitting and rolling are separate skills. The keyboard lab starts its policy on the contact surface. Chapter 6 additionally gates autonomous detection on settled body motion and observations.    Try a gliding shot on passive wheels  This run uses the roller model from initialization to the end. Its four wheels are passive; the same 14 servos propel, steer and brake through leg posture. It never switches to walking or invokes a leg kick. First observe coasting after key release, then practise slowing early so the ball enters the goal while the robot stops before it.  Close the previous scene, then run the command below in the same terminal.  --locomotion rollers  selects the roller physics model and fixed actor, writing to a new output directory.    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py manual \
  --locomotion rollers \
  --seconds 600 \
  --output outputs/manual-rollers-01        Key  Meaning in roller mode      W  Push forward    S  Brake briefly and observe; holding it can reverse motion    Q / E  Turn left / right    Release keys  Coast; this does not guarantee a stop    Space  Run a bounded gliding-shot helper; no leg kick    R / Esc  Reset / exit; A and D do not strafe      Use W, Q and E to bring the ball in front of a wheel, then brief S presses to control approach speed; after alignment, you can also try the Space helper. The roller push input is not a velocity target in metres per second. Compare the modes: a walking shot settles before kicking; a gliding shot transfers momentum through moving contact and then brakes.  Roller mode initializes in a stationary roller posture. Official tyre visuals, mass and inertia are retained; rolling contacts use cylinders 30 mm in diameter and 7.6 mm wide, simplifying the rounded shoulders. Keyboard, football and slope roller experiments share this configuration. Real tyre friction and deformation remain uncalibrated.    How Isaac Sim builds the experiment   Scroll horizontally to view the full diagram    Scene to motion  USD scene：Robot, pitch, ball and goal；Physics：Mass, contact and motors；Policy and input：Keys → ONNX → joint goals       Scene to motion     USD scene  Robot, pitch, ball and  goal   Physics  Mass, contact and motors   Policy and input  Keys → ONNX → joint goals    Rendering, physics and policy have separate roles. A different skill reuses the scene; a different ball position reuses the walking actor.   The robot USD includes joints, collision geometry and inertial properties. The ball has a 5 cm radius and 30 g mass; the goal opening is 38.8 cm wide. Isaac Sim provides the scene and rendering; Isaac Lab configures the Newton physics backend.    Python · 核心代码节选  Full source ↗    cfg.scene.ball = RigidObjectCfg(
    prim_path="{ENV_REGEX_NS}/Ball",
    spawn=sim_utils.SphereCfg(
        radius=0.05,
        mass_props=sim_utils.MassPropertiesCfg(mass=0.03),
        collision_props=sim_utils.CollisionPropertiesCfg(),
        rigid_props=UsdPhysicsRigidBodyCfg(rigid_body_enabled=True),
    ),
    init_state=RigidObjectCfg.InitialStateCfg(pos=(0.0, 0.0, 0.05)),
)
# Apply the shared official-ball asset, goal and floor materials.
scene_profile = configure_football(cfg, style="A")      Fix the scene and hardware contract  The indoor scene uses a 1 × 1.6 m mat, a secured steel-mesh goal measuring 40 cm wide × 20 cm deep × 25 cm high, and an official black-and-white ball with a 10 cm diameter and 30 g mass. This supports short approaches and shots, not arbitrary obstacle avoidance in a confined space. With an assumed 6 mm frame diameter, post centres are 39.4 cm apart and the clear opening is 38.8 × 24.4 cm. Localization uses centre spacing; scoring uses the clear opening.  Choose two football graphics, pale marble or brown wood within the same 1 × 1.6 m area, robot and lighting. The fixed steel-mesh goal has trapezoidal sides and a sloping back, following the product photo. Frame and wires collide; the floor is a rigid plane without foam compression or raised edges. Different textures do not imply calibrated physical friction for each real surface.      A: striped football pitch; B: plain football pitch; C: pale marble; D: brown wood. The same pose isolates appearance; these are not four task outcomes.   The robot uses official Microduck CAD with backlash and full-body collisions. The course pins the XL330 BAM actuator fit, 200 Hz physics and 50 Hz actor updates. The walking actor controls 14 of the 15 physical servos; it does not independently drive the mouth. Full-body collision geometry allows the head, legs and battery to rest on the ground after a fall.  This is a versioned simulation configuration. The camera corresponds to GC2093, but simulation samples at 960 × 540 and 15 Hz with an uncalibrated 70° horizontal field of view. ToF and body IMU models also contain approximations. This does not establish parity with every latest firmware or hardware error, nor validate full deployment on RK3566. Check the real hardware revision, voltage, joint offsets, lens parameters and end-to-end delay before transfer.  Comparison with upstream on 23 October 2026 found no changes to the pinned CAD meshes, base mass/joint parameters or motor fit. This scene adds the official full-body contact configuration. The mechanical viewer retains the Pi Zero 2 W board mesh in the CAD, while current Beta software targets RK3566. The displayed board is not evidence of the latest electronics.    How walking mode switches between gait and kick policies      File  Size  Role      walk.onnx  793,705 bytes, about 0.79 MB  Walking and standing    kick-teacher.onnx  793,685 bytes, about 0.79 MB  Right-foot kick      The walking and kicking combination retains the fixed official weights used in the existing task validation; those files are not the latest browser walking weights. The roller lab separately uses the verified browser roller model. Hardware correspondence, policy identity and task success require separate checks.  Both actors map 61 observations to 14 joint actions through hidden layers of 512, 256 and 128 units with ELU activations. Their input normalization is embedded in ONNX. Keyboard commands set velocity, not individual joint angles. A bounded kick blends back to standing; this lab does not load the course residual actor.                                                                                                         Observation  61       ⋮  Normalize  Hidden 1  512       ⋮  ELU  Hidden 2  256       ⋮  ELU  Hidden 3  128       ⋮  ELU  Action  14       ⋮  Joint actions  Fully connected · inference every 20 ms · no camera images    Circles show a subset of units; numbers give actual dimensions. The official walking and kick actors share this structure but have different weights. The training critic is not shown.     Python · 核心代码节选  Full source ↗    # Read the state once per policy step, then select the active skill.
obs = env.observation_manager.compute(update_history=True)["policy"]
action = walk(obs)

if kick_start is not None:
    phase = (step - kick_start) * 0.02
    weight = 1.0 if phase < 0.14 else max(0.0, 1.0 - (phase - 0.14) / 0.12)
    if weight:
        action = torch.lerp(action, kick(obs), weight)

# The action manager maps network outputs to joint targets.
env.action_manager.process_action(action)    The lab holds the kick for 0.14 s and blends back over 0.12 s. This is a handoff setting, not retraining of the official weights. Small policy files do not imply a small simulator memory footprint.    Terminal  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py inspect-model --model models/walk.onnx      Who decided the next step?   Check your understanding  Which decisions did you make for the robot?   Show explanation  You identified the ball and goal, estimated distance, selected a route and stance, and decided when to kick. Chapter 6 shows an engineered pipeline; Chapters 7–9 explore learned policies and task agents.    Next, inspect the mechanism and the timing between policy and physics.

title: Mechanism and control timing
text: From assembly to components  Microduck is a small biped. Its legs support and move the body, the neck directs its view, and the trunk houses computing, power, and connections. Visual meshes describe appearance. Joints and collision geometry describe permitted motion and contact. These play different roles in simulation.       Open interactive model    Assembled   Exploded  Reset view    Click a part or its label to inspect it  Left-drag to orbit, middle-drag to pan, scroll or pinch to zoom. Use the slider to separate the parts.    Move the separation slider to inspect the leg and head servos. Click their labels to identify the driven joints, then inspect the camera, controller board and battery. Reset to trace the leg joints.   Hardware revision and simulation joints  There are 15 servos: five per leg, four for the head and neck, and one for the beak. The policy drives 14 joints; the beak remains fixed. The CAD retains a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W board mesh; this is not the current Beta RK3566 electronics configuration. Chapters 6–7 connect camera, ToF and IMU data to task observation and learned policies.     Parts, joints, and degrees of freedom  A pen held at its tip can rotate in several directions, while a hinge normally rotates around one fixed axis. Robot joints impose similar constraints. A degree of freedom is an independent variable needed to describe permitted motion; a component count describes physical pieces. The 70 components in this viewer do not imply 70 policy actions.      Region  Active joints  Main role      Each leg  Hip yaw, roll, pitch; knee; ankle: 5 joints  Support the body and place the foot    Neck and head  Neck pitch; head pitch, yaw, roll: 4 joints  Orient the camera and head    Beak  Physical servo; not controlled by this policy  Shown in 3D model, excluded from the 14-action interface      Select a hip servo and inspect its output shaft and nearby bearing. The servo controls an active angle, the bearing supports rotation, and brackets connect adjacent joints. Material, shape, and assembly clearance affect motion. The viewer preserves 3D model detail but does not simulate screw preload, plastic elasticity, or cable forces; it is an anatomy aid rather than manufacturing documentation.    How software moves the mechanism    1 Policy action   2 Joint targets   3 Actuator torque   4 Physics update   5 New observation   A policy does not teleport the robot to a desired position. It outputs actions that become joint targets. Actuators produce torque based on the difference between target and measured state. The resulting motion depends on contact, gravity, inertia, and friction.  The policy runs at 50 Hz and physics at 200 Hz: each action spans four physics steps. Backlash introduces passive joints representing transmission play. Passive joints are not additional policy outputs.    Describe motion with frames      Frame  What is expressed here      World  Pitch, goal, and overall robot position    Body  Forward, lateral, and turn commands; ball relative to the robot    Camera  Image rays and detected target directions    Joint-local  A joint’s axis and angle       Check your understanding  If the head joints stay fixed, is the camera image necessarily stable?   Show explanation  No. Body pitch and roll move the neck and camera. Image stability depends on camera orientation relative to the world, not only on joint angles.      Exercise: trace one load path  Start with the assembled model. Trace a path from the left foot through the ankle, shin, knee, thigh, and hip. Ground support reaches the body through this chain. Explode the assembly and select the servos and brackets around a joint. Identify the fixed housing and the part driven by its output. Explosion offsets are display positions, not physically reachable joint poses.  A servo combines a motor, reduction gears, position feedback, and control electronics. Reaching a target takes time and is limited by torque, speed, friction, and backlash. A policy issuing an angle does not mean the joint instantly reaches it. Chapter 2 observes this difference; Chapter 3 explains how a policy learns around it.   Check your understanding  Does moving the foot farther out in the exploded view change the simulated leg length?   Show explanation  No. The web view explains components. Robot description files define simulated dimensions and joint connections.      What the policy receives and produces  Chapter 1 runs inference with a trained policy. It maps the current observation to 14 joint actions without updating neural-network parameters. Changing the velocity command tests the same model under a different request; it is not training. Choosing a different model file changes the policy.      Observation, in interface order  Width  What it tells the policy      Angular velocity and projected gravity  6  Body rotation and tilt    Relative joint positions  14  Pose relative to the nominal posture    Joint velocities  14  Motion at each joint    Previous action  14  Previous control output and temporal context    Velocity, head, and body commands  3 + 4 + 6  Requested behavior                                                                                                             Observation  61       ⋮  Normalize  Hidden 1  512       ⋮  ELU  Hidden 2  256       ⋮  ELU  Hidden 3  128       ⋮  ELU  Action  14       ⋮  Joint actions  Fully connected · inference every 20 ms · no camera images    Circles show a subset of units; numbers give actual dimensions. The official walking and kick actors share this structure but have different weights. The training critic is not shown.   These values total 61. Reordering joints breaks their meaning even if the input still has 61 entries: the policy might read a knee as a hip. Course entry points preserve ordering, nominal posture, and control timing. Begin by changing commands, duration, and output directories; modify observation construction only after understanding the interface.

title: Learning to walk
text:
One reinforcement-learning loop  The policy receives a vector containing body attitude, angular velocity, joint state, a velocity command, and the previous action. It outputs joint actions, physics advances, and rewards measure progress toward the objective. PPO collects a batch of interactions, updates the policy, and samples again.    1 Observe   2 Sample actions   3 Simulate   4 Compute rewards   5 Update PPO   The environment count is the number of simultaneous robot copies. Iterations repeat collection and optimization. More environments increase parallel sampling and memory demand. A rising training reward means the optimized objective is improving; independent behavior checks are still necessary.    Why PPO looks beyond immediate reward  Lifting a foot can briefly reduce stability while being necessary for forward progress. Reinforcement learning therefore considers return over time rather than just the current reward. A discount factor reduces the weight of more distant rewards, balancing immediate feedback with longer-term consequences.  In PPO, the actor chooses actions and the critic estimates future return. An outcome better than the critic expected receives a positive advantage estimate, encouraging a higher probability for the corresponding action; a worse outcome does the opposite. PPO limits how far an update moves from the old policy to reduce abrupt changes. It does not guarantee that every update improves real task success.  A critic may receive additional simulation information to evaluate trajectories, but the deployed actor must depend only on observations available at runtime. A simulator knowing exact body velocity does not imply that hardware has a perfect velocity sensor. Keep training or scoring ground truth out of the deployed controller.  When designing rewards, list desired behaviors and then consider shortcuts. Rewarding ball motion may encourage body collisions; rewarding stillness may discourage walking. Track both goals and constraints: velocity error, episode length, falls, joint limits, and contact type. This chapter practices the training loop; Chapter 6 tests the complete task definition.    Run a short training exercise    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py train-walk \
  --num-envs 64 \
  --iterations 20 \
  --seed 101 \
  --output outputs/student-walk-01    This is a workflow exercise, not a promise that 20 iterations will learn to walk. Expected result: terminal progress, a new run directory, checkpoints, and an exported policy. Observe loss, return, and episode length without committing to a long training run.    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py tensorboard \
  --logdir outputs/student-walk-01 \
  --port 6006    Open the local TensorBoard address printed in the terminal. Compare reward with episode length. If reward grows while episodes remain short, consider whether the objective rewards a brief action followed by a fall.  Current practice uses full-body contacts, including the head and legs during falls. New outputs are separate experiments; historical learning curves retain their original configuration. Training does not render frames; policy playback uses the shared RTX lighting and materials.    From a smoke run to a longer training run  The 20-iteration exercise checks the pipeline, not convergence. A longer run below uses 1024 environments for 2500 iterations in a new output directory. Judge convergence with curves and independent evaluation, not iteration count alone.    Terminal  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py train-walk \
  --num-envs 1024 --iterations 2500 --seed 101 \
  --output outputs/walking-training-01    Use TensorBoard to compare reward, episode length, falls and velocity error. Use the short-run export in the next section, or explicitly select outputs/walking-training-01/exported/policy.onnx after this longer run. Neither changes the official model.    Explicitly test your own policy  Run the command below in a terminal at the repository root. If it specifies an output directory, use a new one to retain earlier results.    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py walk \
  --model outputs/student-walk-01/exported/policy.onnx \
  --velocity 0.30 0.00 0.00 \
  --seconds 12 \
  --seed 202 \
  --output outputs/student-walk-test-01    Here you deliberately select your own model. Compare support, drift, and falls with the official model from Chapter 1. Later lessons still use  models/walk.onnx ; this export does not change their default.   Go further  To increase the budget, choose a new output directory and try, for example, 1,024 environments and 500 iterations. Check available memory and time first. A saved checkpoint is not a qualification result. Evaluate unseen seeds and retain failures.     Terminal  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py walk \
  --model models/walk.onnx --velocity 0.3 0 0 \
  --seconds 12 --seed 202 \
  --output outputs/official-walk-comparison-01    Match command, duration and seed. Compare falls, distance and actual velocity, then test standing at zero command. One moving demonstration is not a complete skill benchmark.    Why domain randomization matters  Real actuators do not have identical friction, delay, and backlash on every run. Varying parameters in training exposes the policy to more conditions. A narrow range can overfit; an excessively broad range can make learning difficult. Randomization can improve robustness but does not replace hardware testing.   Check your understanding  Why is the highest-reward training episode not an independent test?   Show explanation  It contributed to learning or selection, and reward may differ from task success. Independent testing uses predetermined scenarios and success criteria and counts every outcome.      Checkpoints, curves, and independent tests  Practice starts from random parameters rather than the course walking weights. Each PPO iteration gathers trajectories from several environments and then updates the policy. Rewards combine velocity tracking, body attitude, action smoothness, and contact-related terms. Two policies with similar total rewards may obtain them through accurate motion or simply moving less; inspect both behavior and individual reward terms.   initial.pt  records initialization;  model_*.pt  files are checkpoints;  env.yaml  and  agent.yaml  preserve environment and optimizer settings;  exported/policy.onnx  is the inference export. A checkpoint can contain optimizer state, while ONNX normally preserves the inference graph. They are not interchangeable file formats.  Record the training budget, held-out test seeds, and observed behavior. The 20-iteration exercise teaches sampling, updates, saving, and export. A weak practice policy is no reason to replace downstream course defaults. For a larger budget, keep the earlier run, use a new output directory, and state whether you changed environment count, iteration count, or rewards.   Check your understanding  Does saving only ONNX guarantee an exact training continuation?   Show explanation  No. Exact continuation also needs optimizer, normalization and random states, together with matching configuration. Preserve full checkpoints and training settings.      Will a flat-ground skill handle a slope?  You can now collect rollouts, update PPO, export ONNX and test a policy. Will its foot clearance and balance adjustments work on a slope? Predict the outcome, then test the same policy in Chapter 4.

title: Adapt walking to slopes
text:
Start with a testable question  Do not assume the old actor will fail. Hold the policy, command, duration, friction and initial-state distribution fixed while varying slope. Test traversal and balance, not just a single attractive frame.   Scroll horizontally to view the full diagram    Terrain generalization  Baseline：Same actor: flat/up/down；Isaac Lab training：Sample parallel terrains；Held-out evaluation：Arrival, falls, speed error       Terrain generalization     Baseline  Same actor: flat/up/down   Isaac Lab training  Sample parallel terrains   Held-out evaluation  Arrival, falls, speed  error    Evaluate before adapting. Retain flat-ground ability while testing improvements on slopes.     Build a flat–ramp–landing scene  The surface has a 0.35 m flat approach, a 1 m horizontal ramp, and a landing. Positive angles ascend; negative angles descend. A continuous collision mesh avoids unintended steps. Visual materials do not determine contact dynamics.      The darker surface marks the ramp; gold guides show direction and green marks the target. These visual markings do not change contact physics.              Flat: 0.35 m  Ramp run: 1 m  Landing      h(x) = tan(α) · clip(x − 0.35, 0, 1)    Slope α / °       Adjust the slope to compare ascent and descent. Horizontal and vertical scales match; the landing height changes with the angle.    坡面高度  \[h(x)=\tan(\alpha)\,\operatorname{clip}(x-0.35,0,1)\]     Python · 核心代码节选  Full source ↗    slope = math.tan(math.radians(cfg.slope_deg))
xs = [-48.0, 2.35, 3.35, 52.0]
zs = [0.0, 0.0, slope, slope]
vertices = [(x, y, z) for x, z in zip(xs, zs) for y in [-48.0, 52.0]]
origin = np.array([2.0, 2.0, 0.0])    The mesh origin is (2, 2, 0). Subtracting it places the robot at relative x = 0 and the ramp between x = 0.35 m and 1.35 m. Continuous approach and landing support extends across 100 × 100 m so failures do not fall off a small terrain tile. Isaac Lab’s TerrainGenerator and TerrainImporter share this geometry across visualization, physics tests and parallel training.    Test the official walking policy first  Run the official walking policy on a 5° uphill ramp for 20 seconds. Run the command below from the repository root with a new output directory.    Terminal  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py terrain \
  --model models/walk.onnx \
  --slope 5 --num-envs 1 --seconds 20 --seed 42001 \
  --output outputs/slope-up-05    Without --headless this opens Isaac Sim. Use --num-envs 5 --headless for batched evaluation, and test 0, ±5, ±10 and ±15 degrees in separate output directories. The first 2 s are standing; then the command is 0.25 m/s. Actual speed may differ.  Success requires reaching x ≥ 1.45 m within 20 s with lateral error below 0.3 m and staying upright throughout. A fall remains a failure even if the body later slides across the finish. Reports separate reaching, falls and velocity RMSE.      Slope  Pass  Fall      0°  5/5  0/5    +5°  0/5  0/5    -5°  0/5  5/5    +10°  0/5  0/5    -10°  0/5  5/5    +15°  0/5  0/5    -15°  0/5  5/5      Each angle uses five lightly perturbed starts. Flat trials pass; uphill trials stall without falling; downhill trials fall. This small baseline identifies an adaptation need, not general reliability.    Why flat-ground experience may not transfer  A slope changes foot clearance, gravity along the surface and usable friction. Insufficient clearance or propulsion can stall ascent; downhill landing and balance changes can cause falls. Survival alone misses stalled traversal.    Continue learning across terrain types  Keep the official ONNX unchanged. Initialize a new actor from its weights and normalization, with a fresh critic and optimizer. Mix 25% flat terrain with ascending and descending terrain. Verify initial actor parity before learning.    Terminal  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py train-terrain \
  --model models/walk.onnx \
  --num-envs 256 --iterations 1000 --seed 43001 \
  --output outputs/terrain-training-01    Training slopes are tan(α), not degrees: 0.03–0.22 is about 1.7°–12.4°. Training uses pyramidal and inverted slopes; evaluation uses straight ramps and separate seeds.    Python · 核心代码节选  Full source ↗    sub_terrains = {
    "flat": MeshPlaneTerrainCfg(proportion=0.25),
    "slopes": HfPyramidSlopedTerrainCfg(
        proportion=0.375, slope_range=(0.03, 0.22), platform_width=0.7
    ),
    "descending": HfInvertedPyramidSlopedTerrainCfg(
        proportion=0.375, slope_range=(0.03, 0.22), platform_width=0.7
    ),
}    The fixed terrain weights retain their original training lineage. Current practice runs use the same full-contact robot as the demonstrations, so their contact configuration differs from the historical training and defines a new experiment. Training is physics-only; inspect exported policies in the shared RTX scene.    Balance and direction both matter   第一步：定义有物理含义的误差  \[e_{\omega}=\omega_z-\omega_z^*,\qquad u=\frac{e_{\omega}}{\sigma}\]    第二步：把误差转换为平滑、有界的奖励  \[r_{\omega}=\exp(-u^2)=\exp\!\left[-\left(\frac{\omega_z-\omega_z^*}{0.15}\right)^2\right]\]     Python · 核心代码节选  Full source ↗    def yaw_rate_tracking(env, std=0.15):
    # Match the commanded turn rate without penalizing normal roll/pitch motion.
    velocity = env.scene["robot"].data.root_link_ang_vel_b.torch
    target = env.command_manager.get_command("base_velocity")[:, 2]

    # Squared, normalized error gives a symmetric reward in (0, 1].
    return torch.exp(-((velocity[:, 2] - target) / std).square())

title: Explore community movement skills
text: What else can the same robot learn?  Community projects train jumping and ball balancing using different tasks, rewards and initial states. These demonstrations come from their original simulation environments and do not establish equivalent Newton or hardware performance.      Community jump demonstration in the original four-times slow motion. Observe takeoff, flight, landing and the standing handoff.       Community ball-balancing demonstration: watch the moving support surface and continuous posture corrections.       Skill  Observations and actions  Rewards and completion      Jumping  Body state and a jump command → joint actions  Height, landing posture and recovery    Basketball balance  Robot and ball state → joint actions  Balance, relative position and survival    Walking  Body state and velocity command → joint actions  Speed tracking, stability, energy and smoothness      Isaac Sim supplies props and contact geometry; Isaac Lab organizes observations, rewards and reset distributions. Equal observation dimensions do not guarantee compatibility: the jump policy repurposes a command field as a launch trigger.    Define a skill’s boundaries  Walking continuously accepts velocity commands. A kick is a short skill with a start and an end. Integrating it into an autonomous task requires entry conditions, a defined exit state, and a way to stop when conditions are unsafe.      Phase  What to check      Jumping  Body state and a jump command → joint actions  Height, landing posture and recovery    Basketball balance  Robot and ball state → joint actions  Balance, relative position and survival    Walking  Body state and velocity command → joint actions  Speed tracking, stability, energy and smoothness        Why ONNX files are not interchangeable  ONNX is a model representation, not a universal robot-skill protocol. The walking model takes 61 inputs, while the kicking residual takes 62. Both output 14 numbers, yet they are not interchangeable. Input ordering, additional state, action scaling, teacher blending, and termination conditions are all part of the runtime contract.  Loading a model only establishes that its format is readable. Units, joint order and scaling must match the controller. The  models page  lists the fixed weights and their roles. Chapter 6 shows the complete task assembled from these skills.  Watch the kick in three phases: before it, inspect ball and support-foot positions; during it, identify whether contact comes from the foot or another body part; afterwards, inspect recovery of support. Pause the video in each phase and describe the entry and completion conditions. This is more informative than asking only whether the ball moved.    Describe a skill by its contract  Describe a skill using entry conditions, observations, actions, and exit conditions. A kick requires a useful right-foot ball position, goal alignment, stable support, and fresh target information. Execution combines the kicking teacher with a residual correction. It must then return to a stable standing or walking state; touching the ball alone does not finish the task.  A residual adds a constrained correction to an existing action. This reduces what must be learned from scratch but inherits the teacher’s operating range. Starting a local kick far from the ball does not make it search or approach. Navigation creates a valid handoff state; the skill performs its local action.   Check your understanding  The robot is beside the ball, but its remembered position has expired. Should the kick start immediately?   Show explanation  No. Observe again and confirm the entry conditions. Proximity alone does not guarantee valid inputs.      Executing a skill is not completing a task  We currently tell the robot when to move or kick. Joint and IMU feedback support balance, but the policy does not decide where the ball is or which route to take. Next we review a complete perception/planning pipeline, then consider how learned models can take on more decisions.

title: From engineered pipelines to intelligent robots
text: How the engineered method scores  The earlier chapters provide walking, skating and kicking skills. A complete task must also decide where to look, where to move, when to contact the ball and how to recover. This chapter is a guided overview: no installation, code execution or position calculations are required.   Scroll horizontally to view the full diagram    People design the decision flow; existing policies execute motion.  Observe: Camera, ToF and IMU → Locate and plan: Ball, goal and approach route → Align and act: Walking, kicking or skating → Check the outcome: Goal, fall, stopping and recovery           Observe  Camera, ToF and IMU   Locate and plan  Ball, goal and approach route   Align and act  Walking, kicking or skating   Check the outcome  Goal, fall, stopping and recovery    People design the decision flow; existing policies execute motion. Camera projection and frame transforms relate image targets to the robot. A task prior—stand behind the ball and face the goal—defines the approach target. These calculations translate positions and directions; we omit their derivation here. Walking uses ROS 2 Nav2/Navfn planning with a custom tracker; skating uses visual feedback. Isaac ROS offers integration options for perception, but it is not running in this experiment.    Watch a walking shot      A complete walking development example, including observation, repeated alignment, kicking and recovery. The observer view is re-rendered from recorded physics with the original synchronized camera inset. One success is not a reliability estimate.   The look-down and alignment cycles are real controller behavior. Short turns are followed by settling and fresh near-ball observations; a changed heading error can trigger another cycle. Continuous observation, improved turn braking and separate entry/exit thresholds could reduce switching, but require paired physical tests. The complete real-time sequence remains visible.    Watch a gliding shot      Gliding development example: contact at 6.79 s, whole-ball crossing at 8.13 s, then settling before the goal. The robot stays on its wheels throughout; no leg-kick transition occurs. The re-rendered observer view is synchronized with the original camera.   The decision rules differ: skating requires approach and braking control; walking must enter the kicking policy in a suitable pose. A different task requires new handoff rules.    Separate demonstrations from evaluation      New 10 cm-ball scene  Independent full tasks  Observed limitation      Walking shot  0/4  No falls; observation or handoff failed    Gliding shot  1/4; goals 2/4  Stopping or goal-base localization failed      Each group has four predeclared trials, one new seed per floor. Floor and seed change together, so these trials do not establish a causal floor effect. Detection mAP50 is 0.978, yet the full task remains inconsistent: recognition, geometric estimation and execution are different problems. Historical scene scores are kept separate.    Learn actions and how to organize them  Engineered pipelines are interpretable and easy to inspect step by step. They also require people to specify stages, thresholds and recovery. Requests such as moving the ball elsewhere or going around a chair create more integration work. Learned policies and reusable skills can carry more of that experience. The following chapters explain the integration design and inspected interfaces; they do not claim a completed GR00T or ASPIRE Microduck football experiment.

title: Teach GR00T from demonstrations
text: Express the task through goals and demonstrations  A language goal such as “send the ball into the goal,” paired with successful demonstrations, offers another way to specify the task. A vision-language-action model uses images, instructions and robot state to predict a short action sequence. Data can capture decisions previously distributed across looking, alignment and approach rules.   Scroll horizontally to view the full diagram    GR00T repeatedly observes and predicts short action segments in a feedback loop.  Inputs: Images + instruction + robot state → GR00T N1.7: Interpret context and predict an action chunk → Robot control: Execute a short prefix; maintain stability → Fresh observation: Reconsider the next action            Inputs  Images + instruction + robot state   GR00T N1.7  Interpret context and predict an action chunk   Robot control  Execute a short prefix; maintain stability   Fresh observation  Reconsider the next action    GR00T repeatedly observes and predicts short action segments in a feedback loop.  Inputs: Images + instruction + robot state → GR00T N1.7: Interpret context and predict an action chunk → Robot control: Execute a short prefix; maintain stability → Fresh observation: Reconsider the next action            Inputs  Images + instruction + robot state   GR00T N1.7  Interpret context and predict an action  chunk   Robot control  Execute a short prefix; maintain stability   Fresh observation  Reconsider the next action    GR00T repeatedly observes and predicts short action segments in a feedback loop.   Action prediction and whole-task planning are related but distinct. An action chunk is not a globally collision-free path. Longer tasks also need goal management, checks and recovery, which the next chapter addresses.    Use the current public GR00T N1.7  As checked on 26 October 2026, the current public release is  GR00T N1.7 , with base checkpoint  nvidia/GR00T-N1.7-3B . It uses a Cosmos-Reason2-2B / Qwen3-VL backbone and an action head; that does not mean Cosmos 3 is already part of this model. Official workflows support custom-robot fine-tuning and policy serving.  Microduck is not a pretrained embodiment validated here. SO-101 arm actions, the model’s tensor capacity and Microduck’s fourteen controlled joints are not interchangeable. Every action needs a defined physical meaning, unit, rate, normalization and controller interface.    What transfers from the SO-101 course  The SO-101 course supplies a reusable workflow: teleoperate, record synchronized images/state/actions, prepare LeRobot data, adapt GR00T, then evaluate simulation and hardware separately. Lighting, robot color and mat variations broaden visual coverage. The transferable part is this data and evaluation method; vial-manipulation weights are not a football policy.      SO-101 lesson  Microduck counterpart      Synchronize cameras and joints  Retain body motion, gaze and action timing    Demonstrate grasp, place and recovery  Demonstrate approach, contact, braking and recovery    Evaluate sim and real separately  Test new scenes before hardware calibration    Vary appearance  Cover home lighting, backgrounds and floors        Define what the model may control  A practical first research route retains the locomotion policies and learns bounded body-motion and gaze requests, reducing hand-written observation/alignment/advance transitions. Walking and skating have different command semantics: use separate configurations or an explicit mode condition. A gliding shot remains in roller mode throughout. A higher-level controller can request a kicking skill; a continuous number is not automatically a validated discrete skill switch.  Learning joint actions is another route, with greater data and validation demands because balance and contact must also be learned. N1.7’s new-embodiment example supports non-end-effector actions. Definable fields, however, do not establish a learned fourteen-joint football policy. Validate the hierarchical interface before selecting the training target.    What makes demonstrations useful   Scroll horizontally to view the full diagram    Demonstration quality, action alignment and held-out evaluation matter beyond video quantity.  Collect: Starts, instructions, floors and recovery → Align: Current images/state → subsequent actions → Split: Group by episode, room and layout → Adapt and evaluate: Start short, then expand task scope           Collect  Starts, instructions, floors and recovery   Align  Current images/state → subsequent actions   Split  Group by episode, room and layout   Adapt and evaluate  Start short, then expand task scope    Demonstration quality, action alignment and held-out evaluation matter beyond video quantity.  Collect: Starts, instructions, floors and recovery → Align: Current images/state → subsequent actions → Split: Group by episode, room and layout → Adapt and evaluate: Start short, then expand task scope           Collect  Starts, instructions, floors and recovery   Align  Current images/state → subsequent actions   Split  Group by episode, room and layout   Adapt and evaluate  Start short, then expand task scope    Demonstration quality, action alignment and held-out evaluation matter beyond video quantity.   Existing logs contain images, joint state, inertial observations and executed actions, but one successful episode is far from sufficient. Keep success, failure and corrective demonstrations explicitly labeled; ordinary imitation learning must not treat every failed action as a correct target. Distinguish raw policy outputs, actions after gaze overrides and actual motor targets.  The head camera moves, and images/actions have different sampling rates. Align timestamps and observation ages without using future images for past actions. Do not split neighboring frames from one episode across train and test. Hold out complete rooms or layouts to assess unfamiliar homes.    Readiness and the next experiment  The official custom-embodiment configuration, data format and policy interface have been reviewed. Existing roller logs provide 163 image/state frames aligned with entries in 652 action records; 97 actions differ from the raw network output after executor corrections. This checks 163 one-step pairs at 12.5 Hz camera capture and 50 Hz action recording. Official shape validators and added timing/dimension checks pass; future multi-step action chunks remain unchecked. N1.7 weights were not loaded and no inference or fine-tuning ran. Task language, action-conversion configuration and LeRobot export are still needed for training.  This probe uses 14-dimensional low-level action records. The proposed high-level velocity/skill route still needs its own labels and executor; validating one does not validate the other. The visual backbone has model-access requirements. Keep future training dependencies separate from the existing Newton environment. See the  readiness scope and remaining requirements .  For the next experiment, fix one locomotion mode and one short task, collect successful and corrective demonstrations, and evaluate unseen starts and rooms. Keep robot, props, sensors and success criteria identical across baselines; measure scoring, falls, stopping and observation cycles. This establishes whether learning actually reduces repeated corrections.

title: Organize tasks and accumulate skills with ASPIRE
text: A reasoning model needs executable robot interfaces  “Go around the chair and send the ball into the goal” combines goal interpretation, subtask organization and motion. A model can propose and revise a plan, while controllers maintain balance and handle contact. A complete plan may require both a high-level sequence and a geometric route; prose alone does not supply either validated execution or collision avoidance.   Scroll horizontally to view the full diagram    Connect reasoning, skill execution and feedback while retaining continuous motor control.  Task agent: Interpret the goal; choose the next step → Skill interface: Observe, move, contact and stop → Action policy: GR00T or existing motor policies → Feedback: Images, progress, failures and outcome predicates            Task agent  Interpret the goal; choose the next step   Skill interface  Observe, move, contact and stop   Action policy  GR00T or existing motor policies   Feedback  Images, progress, failures and outcome  predicates    Connect reasoning, skill execution and feedback while retaining continuous motor control.  Task agent: Interpret the goal; choose the next step → Skill interface: Observe, move, contact and stop → Action policy: GR00T or existing motor policies → Feedback: Images, progress, failures and outcome predicates            Task agent  Interpret the goal; choose the next step   Skill interface  Observe, move, contact and stop   Action policy  GR00T or existing motor policies   Feedback  Images, progress, failures and outcome  predicates    Connect reasoning, skill execution and feedback while retaining continuous motor control.     ASPIRE: turn attempts into reusable experience  ASPIRE uses code-as-policy: an agent generates control programs, inspects multimodal execution traces, diagnoses failures, revises code and retains validated experience in a skill library. This learning primarily updates programs and skill knowledge, rather than necessarily updating neural weights. The public October 2026 v1.0 workflow includes iterative debugging and evolutionary search.   Scroll horizontally to view the full diagram    Revise from execution feedback and reuse skills after validation.  Propose: Retrieve skills and generate a program → Execute and observe: Record images, actions, states and outcomes → Diagnose and revise: Locate failure and change the next attempt → Retain: Add skills after development validation            Propose  Retrieve skills and generate a program   Execute and observe  Record images, actions, states and outcomes   Diagnose and revise  Locate failure and change the next attempt   Retain  Add skills after development validation    Revise from execution feedback and reuse skills after validation.  Propose: Retrieve skills and generate a program → Execute and observe: Record images, actions, states and outcomes → Diagnose and revise: Locate failure and change the next attempt → Retain: Add skills after development validation            Propose  Retrieve skills and generate a program   Execute and observe  Record images, actions, states and outcomes   Diagnose and revise  Locate failure and change the next attempt   Retain  Add skills after development validation    Revise from execution feedback and reuse skills after validation.   For example, missing goal-post bases on a pale floor can prompt inspection of images and failure records, followed by another viewpoint or a revised perception interface. A program exiting normally is not a goal, and redefining scoring to pass a trial is not an improvement. The reusable output is a tested method.    Adapting the framework to Microduck      Interface  Reusable foundation  Remaining integration      Observation  RGB, ToF, IMU and joint records  Consistent timing, frames and observation age    Action  Walking, skating, kicking and stopping  Bounded calls, timeouts, cancellation and mode semantics    Outcome  Contact, crossing, fall and recovery checks  Diagnostic feedback plus independent scoring    Skill library  Existing control and failure knowledge  Validate new programs on unseen starts/scenes      Official examples target LIBERO-Pro, Robosuite, BEHAVIOR-1K and documented real-arm systems. There is no ready Microduck adapter for this course. Renaming arm joints does not turn end-effector control into biped control. Reuse ASPIRE’s exploration and skill-library approach while implementing body-motion and football interfaces for Newton.    How ASPIRE and GR00T can cooperate  Start by letting ASPIRE call existing motor skills to study task organization. Once a Microduck GR00T adaptation is validated, learned skills can replace selected action components. GR00T maps current observations to actions; ASPIRE organizes goals, calls, checks and revisions. This is a proposed integration, not an officially delivered Microduck stack.  Stable skill interfaces and retained experience reduce repeated task programming. The robot still needs the physical capability for a task: a new prompt alone cannot guarantee pickup without suitable grasping hardware. New demonstrations, skills or tools may still be necessary.    Extension: where Agnes Harness fits      Aspect  ASPIRE  Agnes Harness      Focus  Refine robot programs and skills through execution  Connect models, tools, task state and devices    Reuse  Validated robotic skill libraries  Skills, sessions and execution records    Current scope  Robotic exploration/research workflows  Developer-preview general agent harness    Course role  Main task-agent methodology  Optional device-integration comparison      They share concepts but are not equivalent products. Agnes’s MHS device integration and plugins merit study, but the inspected public main branch contains no ready Microduck adapter. We keep it as an extension rather than repeat the agent loop in another full chapter.  The linked  Microduck community demo  is a useful reference for questions about action tools, completion checks and recovery. Its page was unavailable in this review environment; its implementation and autonomy level have not been independently verified or counted as course results.    Feasible with an adapter and independent evaluation  The method and open interfaces are promising. A Microduck execution bridge, skill library and autonomous exploration trials remain to be implemented. Begin with observe, bounded movement, stop and check, then extend to football. Separate development and held-out seeds, bound trial budgets and record success, recovery and model-call costs.

title: Cover different homes with Cosmos and Isaac
text: What changes in another home  These variations matter. Warm light, backlighting and shadows change the ball’s appearance; walls, tiles and furniture change its background. Narrow passages change routes, while carpet and smooth floors change motion and braking. Visual generalization, spatial planning and dynamics adaptation need separate treatment.      Variation  Primary effect  Useful evaluation      Lighting, color, background  Perception and visual policies  Test new appearance with consistent geometry/actions    Layout, occlusion, starts  Observation strategy and routes  Closed-loop tasks and collisions in new layouts    Friction, tyres, ball mass, latency  Contact, propulsion and braking  Physics ranges and hardware measurements    Instructions and goals  Task understanding and skill selection  Language variation and held-out task combinations        What Cosmos 3 provides  Cosmos 3 is a public omnimodal world-model family covering language, images, video, audio and actions. Reasoner, Generator and specialized policy/simulation variants support scene understanding, candidate scenario generation and action/future-state modeling. Its scope extends beyond background replacement.  For Microduck, initial uses include visual-data expansion and failure analysis. Preserve robot, goal and ball geometry while generating candidate room appearances, then inspect shape, occlusion and temporal consistency. Where depth or segmentation conditioning is required, compare the actual interfaces of specialized models such as Cosmos-Transfer2.5 as well.  A plausible scoring video is not an executable action trajectory. Imitation data require action labels consistent with images, states and timing. A changed ball size, post position or contact time can invalidate the original actions. Cosmos policy/action variants likewise need embodiment adaptation; a DROID specialization is not a Microduck policy.    Generation, physics, learning and orchestration   Scroll horizontally to view the full diagram    Connect data generation, physical validation and policy learning.  Cosmos: Understand worlds; generate or assess candidate data → Isaac Sim + Newton: Generate simulated sensor data; advance contact/motion → Isaac Lab / GR00T: Collect data; train or adapt policies → Arena + OSMO: Compose evaluations and compute workflows           Cosmos  Understand worlds; generate or assess  candidate data   Isaac Sim + Newton  Generate simulated sensor data; advance  contact/motion   Isaac Lab / GR00T  Collect data; train or adapt policies   Arena + OSMO  Compose evaluations and compute workflows    Connect data generation, physical validation and policy learning.  Cosmos: Understand worlds; generate or assess candidate data → Isaac Sim + Newton: Generate simulated sensor data; advance contact/motion → Isaac Lab / GR00T: Collect data; train or adapt policies → Arena + OSMO: Compose evaluations and compute workflows           Cosmos  Understand worlds; generate or assess  candidate data   Isaac Sim + Newton  Generate simulated sensor data; advance  contact/motion   Isaac Lab / GR00T  Collect data; train or adapt policies   Arena + OSMO  Compose evaluations and compute workflows    Connect data generation, physical validation and policy learning.   Cosmos also has world-simulation and policy variants. This course retains Newton for physical evidence of contact, scoring and stopping. OSMO orchestrates workflows; it does not automatically reconcile incompatible action spaces into a common learning target.    Robot × scene × task: Isaac Lab-Arena  Isaac Lab-Arena directly addresses composition. It separates Scene, Embodiment (robot, sensors and actions), and Task (objective and predicates), then builds Isaac Lab environments. It organizes evaluation across layouts, robots and tasks and registers environments for learning/data workflows. The main branch inspected on October 26, 2026 targets Isaac Lab 3.0 / Isaac Sim 6.2 and remains early-stage software; its dependencies differ from release/0.3.1.  Arena provides policy clients including GR00T and Cosmos-related adapters and supports Newton selection. Microduck still needs its own embodiment, football task and action contract. Combinations must satisfy task capabilities. Concurrent evaluation does not itself train a single policy for every robot.    Design an evaluation matrix      Four floors    Three lighting conditions    Three indoor layouts    Walking and skating, evaluated separately   Fresh seeds per combination      This only counts combinations; it launches no simulation or training. Unchecking a factor fixes it to one condition.   Walking and skating are modes of one robot and are evaluated separately here; they are not two physical embodiments. The count describes an experiment design, not completed runs or universal compatibility.    How to test whether randomization helps  Keep a baseline with no added randomization, then separately add appearance, layout and measured dynamics variation while controlling demonstration count, training budget and evaluation criteria. Hold out rooms, layouts or combinations. Keep failed trials rather than replace them with successful retries.  Measure full scoring and settling, falls, route collisions, observation cycles and completion time, not just detection scores. Current failures also involve geometry extraction and braking. Visual randomization may improve observations without fixing stopping control. Target the observed failure before scaling training.    Next: a small, comparable experiment  Choose one locomotion mode, keep the official 10 cm ball and goal fixed, and use the two football floors, marble and wood with controlled lighting, then a small set of indoor layouts. Keep goal-frame material fixed. After aligning simulated sensor data with executed action records, select one initial experiment: GR00T adaptation, ASPIRE skill exploration or Cosmos data expansion, rather than change everything together.  The course reviews methods, interfaces and existing record fields, and illustrates combination design. No new GR00T, ASPIRE, Cosmos or Arena training/control experiment has run. Independent closed-loop results should guide subsequent data and compute investment.

These weights support Chapters 1–5 and the Chapter 6 baseline. GR00T and Cosmos foundation models are not bundled. Future adaptation requires separate model access under the applicable terms and an isolated environment.    Practice data and your outputs   datasets/scene-sample/  is a small image-and-label practice set for detector inference and short training. It is not enough to establish real-world generalization. Student checkpoints and logs belong in  outputs/ ; do not copy them over the course files in  models/ .    Sources and usage terms  Robot geometry, community policies, and dependencies retain their source terms. The course-code license does not override third-party asset licenses. Before redistributing changes, read the repository’s  attribution and license notices .

title: Troubleshooting
text:
Start with the environment report  Run the command below in a terminal at the repository root. If it specifies an output directory, use a new one to retain earlier results.    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py doctor
python3 scripts/workshop.py verify-models    The first failure is more useful than repeatedly launching a full training run. Check the repository directory, the selected runtime, and all model checks.    Common issues      Symptom  What to check      No GUI window  Use the GPU desktop terminal and check DISPLAY and the driver. A remote text shell is not a graphical desktop.    First launch is slow  Check for downloads and compilation. Allow initialization and avoid starting duplicate instances.    Output directory exists  Choose a new run name and preserve the previous result.    Out of memory  Reduce training environments or detector batch size. Avoid concurrent simulations.    Model hash mismatch  Restore the repository model and check for accidental overwrites.    Practice policy walks poorly  A short run teaches the workflow. Inspect reward, episode length, and evaluation. Continue with fixed models.    Robot stops or does not score  Inspect the task report and observation validity. Stopping can be appropriate when information is missing; it is not a goal.        Inspect a run  Run the command below in a terminal at the repository root. If it specifies an output directory, use a new one to retain earlier results.    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py report --run outputs/football-01    When reporting an issue, include the command, seed, environment report, and first error. A success/failure label alone is not enough. Do not include passwords or access tokens.

title: Further learning and references
text: Robotics and simulation  Begin with task observations, actions, and rewards, then explore physics and sensors. Course commands target fixed versions; current documentation may describe newer versions. Check the version before applying changes.    Suggested extensions   Vary the Chapter 3 training budget and compare on the same held-out seeds.  Compare the two Chapter 6 modes: which failures concern observation, action or handoff?  Use Chapter 7 to identify shared data-workflow steps and different action interfaces for Microduck and SO-101.  Use the Chapter 9 counter to plan held-out room evaluation and separate training from test conditions.
